article.title: [gizmodo.com] AI-driven flaw discovery strains patching as outages hit US services
article.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

AI tools are rapidly uncovering software vulnerabilities and helping automate cyberattacks as outages disrupt U.S. email, flight operations, banking services and an internal National Security Agency communications network. Cybersecurity experts have linked some disruptions to rushed fixes for newly found flaws, but Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said the incidents were separate operational problems and officials had no indication of malicious activity or a coordinated attack. Hackers are also using AI to automate attacks. The FBI said hackers used the Artex AI framework in attacks worldwide, with some gaining privileged access in under three hours, while Palo Alto Networks linked another framework, Cairn, to 25 operations against at least 19 organizations. Researchers also used AI to find Java4Shell, a flaw in Java’s Base64 decoding library that could let an attacker execute commands on a vulnerable server. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency urged organizations to patch it. U.S. regulators sent inquiries to banks affected by outages, and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency plans a deeper review of the incidents. Canonical, the company behind Ubuntu, is separately offering AI-generated fixes to Ubuntu Pro customers through an optional early-release channel before its engineers complete normal review and testing.

article.title: [bmj.com] Study finds limited code sharing as medical AI oversight faces scrutiny
article.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

Researchers from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and Dana-Farber Cancer Institute reviewed nearly 4,000 clinical prediction studies and found that only about one in eight reported sharing code. Many public repositories also lacked documentation or files needed to run and check the analyses. The findings are intended to inform a guideline on reusable research code. A physician writing in The BMJ urged Utah to publish independently assessed counts of missed escalation cases before allowing AI-generated acne prescriptions to be reviewed after issuance rather than before. In South Korea, Doctors for a Fair Society called for scrutiny of possible AI-assisted cheating in a medical-school entrance exam, while the group’s leader cautioned against treating an individual’s high score or educational background as proof of wrongdoing.

Many public repositories also lacked documentation or files needed to run and check the

Many public repositories also lacked documentation or files needed to run and check the analyses. The findings are intended to inform a guideline on reusable research code (lavx.hu). In South Korea, Doctors for a Fair Society called for scrutiny of possible AI-assisted cheating in a medical-school entrance exam, while the group’s leader cautioned against treating an individual’s high score or educational background as proof of wrongdoing (kormedi.com). Study sample: Researchers drew from PubMed Central’s open-access collection and included studies that developed, updated or validated prediction models and cited the TRIPOD or TRIPOD+AI reporting checklists (lavx.hu). Safety reporting: Utah’s agreement sets a target of zero material missed escalations and requires audits of encounters the AI did not flag, but does not specify a count or denominator for quarterly public reporting (bmj.com). Exam scrutiny: The Korean group asked the consortium that administers the MDEET medical-school entrance exam for an official response. The test was not among 528 national qualification exams slated for a government-wide investigation (kormedi.com).

article.title: [stpetersburg.usf.edu] Study finds drought could cut cactus habitat by 80% by 2100
article.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

An international research team analyzed nearly 1,000 cactus species and found that more than a quarter could lose at least 80% of their suitable habitat by 2100 if severe droughts intensify. The researchers added drought projections to climate models, which commonly use long-term temperature and rainfall averages, and combined them with biodiversity records, field observations and community-science data. The projected losses could qualify affected species as Critically Endangered under criteria set by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), more than doubling the number of cacti in that category. Researchers say drought may also reduce growth or flowering without immediately killing plants, compounding threats from habitat destruction and illegal collection. The findings are expected to inform updated IUCN Red List assessments; the team says further research is needed to determine which life stages and biological processes drought affects.

Regional hotspots: Projected diversity declines could be especially severe in cactus-rich areas of Chile, Peru and northeastern Brazil (usf.edu). Existing pressures: More than 30% of cactus species are already threatened with extinction (usf.edu). Saguaro reproduction: In the Sonoran Desert, prolonged drought has been associated with saguaros flowering less often, reducing opportunities for reproduction (grist.org). Model shift: When severe drought was included, the share of cactus species described as “sick” by lead author Michiel Pillet, a conservation ecologist at the University of South Florida, rose from about six in 10 to seven in 10 (azfamily.com).

article._excerpt: The highest attendance for this year's Performances in Park at Boitanio Park in Williams Lake was on Aug. 6 with 312 people. It was another successful year of Performances in the Park despite attendance being down, according to the Central Cariboo Arts and Culture Society. At a Nov. 25 Central Cariboo Joint Committee meeting, executive director Melissa Normandin provided an overview of the free, family-friendly summer concert series that brought live music and cultural performances in Boitanio Park for Williams Lake residents and visitors from July 9 to Aug. 27. An average of 219 attendees were welcomed each evening, marking a small decrease from the 2025 season that had an average weekly attendance of 237. “Attendance was a bit down and I’m going to blame the weather for that,” Normandin said. Of the 16 different performers or acts participating in this year’s Performances in the Park seven were local. A total program budget of $36,155 supported through diversified funding sources including local government, community sponsorships and in-kind contributions. In June, Williams Lake First Nation was added as a core funding partner with the City of Williams Lake and Cariboo Regional District for a three year term that includes an annual payment of $22,000 to the society for eight summer events. Normandin said their budget dollars were pretty consistent with previous years, and if they had more they could probably review some different asks received from the community including shade and covered areas. Cleanliness and adequately supplied washroom facilities throughout the evening was another challenge, along with glass, and broken bottles and garbage. “We can tackle that, and hopefully work with the city on that,” Normandin said. Mayor Surinderpal Rathor said he attended every concert and encouraged organizers to keep up the good work. The highest attendance was on Aug. 6 featuring Sassafrass (Kimberly Kavanagh) along with Punjabi Gidha and Punjabi Bhangra performances

article.title: [medicalxpress.com] Study links very large and small waists to higher death risk
article.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

A study of more than 17 million South Korean adults found that both unusually large and unusually small waist measurements were associated with a higher risk of death across weight and age groups. The lowest observed risk was associated with waist circumferences of 80–94 centimeters in men and 75–89 centimeters in women. The association between waist circumference and death risk was stronger at older ages, especially among women 75 and older. Researchers analyzed routine health-check measurements from 2009–10 and tracked survival for nearly 14 years, through June 30, 2024. The study was observational and cannot show that waist size causes death. Among people with normal weight or overweight whose waist circumference was high for their body mass index (BMI), reducing waist circumference without necessarily losing weight appeared to offer a greater survival benefit than losing weight while reducing waist circumference, the authors said.

Risk increments: Among participants whose waists were at or above the average for their sex, age and BMI, each additional 5 centimeters was associated with a 16% higher death risk in men and 14% in women (medicalxpress.com, elnacional.com.do). Other risk factors: Gastroenterologist Olga Sukhareva said insulin resistance can occur in people with low body weight and cited factors including low muscle mass, inactivity, diet, genetics and polycystic ovary syndrome (rambler.ru).

article._excerpt: In the wake of the Bald Range wildfire, an international study is seeking volunteers from the South Okanagan for a new treatment method for those dealing with post-traumatic stress disorder. Penticton in the South Okanagan is one of four B.C. communities, alongside Kelowna, Kamloops and North Vancouver, selected to participate in the study. The impacts of the Bald Range wildfire, which saw thousands of people forced out of their homes in the Okanagan, left behind more than physical scars on the region. About 150 structures, including homes and accessory structures, were destroyed within the Regional District of Okanagan Similkameen and District of Summerland as a result of the fast-moving Aug. 7 blaze. Faulder was particularly hard hit by the fire, as the closest community to the origin point. The cause of the fire remains under investigation. “PTSD touches so many people in our community: first responders, people who’ve survived accidents or violence, families who lost homes to fire. Being part of rigorous, closely supervised research means people in the South Okanagan have a real voice in what the next generation of care looks like,” said Dr. Linda Grasswick, principal investigator for the study in Penticton. Medical Arts Health Research Group is conducting the study under Health Canada and research ethics oversight. The treatment will explore an investigational form of psilocybin, one of the naturally occurring compounds found in many so-called “magic” mushrooms. Adults living with PTSD in the South Okanagan who would like to learn more can contact the study team confidentially at (888) 490-4320 or visit www.healthresearch.ca. Reaching out does not commit anyone to participate. Those interested will be screened by a doctor to determine whether the study is a safe and appropriate fit. Participants will receive care and support from a dedicated study team throughout, and study-related visits, assessments, and the investigational medication are provided at no cost.

article.title: [cbc.ca] B.C. floods force evacuations, shelter orders as roads close
article.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Heavy rain and flooding across British Columbia’s South Coast prompted shelter-in-place advisories near Squamish and in Pemberton Valley, while evacuation orders covered parts of Pemberton and Lil’wat Nation on Thursday, Nov. 12. Some areas received more than 300 millimetres of rain in 48 hours, and floodwater closed Highway 99 east of Pemberton and roads near Squamish. The entire Village of Pemberton was under an evacuation alert. Evacuation orders also remained in effect in Zeballos, where flooding and landslide risks threatened about 30 properties. The release of water from the Cheakamus Dam flooded roads near Squamish and was intended to make room in the reservoir for more rain. Officials expected river levels to crest Thursday and then recede. Rain eased in some areas, but Vancouver Island remained under rainfall and flood warnings, and forecasters were tracking more storm systems expected over the weekend.

article.title: [agri-mutuel.com] French institute plans AI farm adviser as Deere expands data tool
article.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

France’s public agricultural research institute INRAE plans to build an AI assistant using verified scientific data to help farmers respond to climate change and other pressures. The project awaits approval for €1.2 million in France 2030 funding, with a first version planned for farmer testing within 18 months. Separately, John Deere expanded access to its free JD assistant on Nov. 16, linking it to the company’s Operations Center farm-management platform. INRAE’s proposed assistant would tailor guidance to a farm’s location, practices, soil, expected water resources and finances, while Deere’s tool searches and analyzes information already recorded about a user’s fields, machinery and farm operations. INRAE says the project has demonstrated answers to simple queries and aims to handle more complex questions; farmer testing depends on the funding decision.

article.title: [simon42.com] Home Assistant Beta enables camera recordings with HomeKit Secure Video in Apple Home
article.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

The second beta of the smart home software Home Assistant 2026.12 makes it possible for the first time to connect cameras via the HomeKit Bridge and save their recordings with HomeKit Secure Video in Apple Home. Until now, the Bridge only transmitted live video; additional software was needed for recordings. Requirements include an Apple home hub, an iCloud+ subscription, a motion sensor, and setting up the camera as a standalone HomeKit accessory. Recording must be enabled separately for each camera. Recordings only start when motion is detected. As a result, the first few seconds may be missing. Home Assistant recommends H.264 streams, since conversion via FFmpeg uses processing power. In the developer test, an H.265 source failed to meet the Apple home hub’s time limit. The final version is planned for December 2, 2026; until then, beta features may still change.
